description: Aihole, in Bagalkot district of Karnataka, was an early Chalukya temple-building centre and holds roughly ten Jain monuments dating from about the 6th to the 12th century, according to Wikipedia. The best known is the Meguti Jain temple on a hilltop above the town. The Archaeological Survey of India dates its completion to about 634 CE from an inscription on its eastern wall, the Aihole Prashasti, composed by the Jain poet Ravikirti in praise of the Chalukya king Pulakeshin II. The temple has a pillared porch, a two-part vestibule and a sanctum with a circumambulatory passage; a stair in the front hall leads to an upper shrine whose tower is ruined. Wikipedia describes it as dedicated to the Tirthankara Mahavira. Other Jain remains include the rock-cut Meena Basti cave, a Late Chalukya group at Charanthi Matha dated by Wikipedia to the 12th century, and temples of the Yoginarayana group, dated there to about the 11th century.

description: Aihole is a village in Bagalkot district, Karnataka, on the Malaprabha River, with more than 120 stone and cave temples spread over roughly five square kilometres, according to Wikipedia. It was an early Chalukya centre, and most surviving monuments date from the 7th to 10th centuries, though the site's span is given as the 4th to 12th centuries. Hindu shrines predominate, alongside a few Jain monuments and one Buddhist. Well-known structures include the apsidal Durga temple with its rekha-nagara tower; the Lad Khan temple, a Shiva shrine named after a later Muslim commander who used it; and the Meguti Jain temple, whose inscription of 634 CE, composed by Ravikirti, praises the Chalukya king Pulakeshin II. The 6th-century Ravanaphadi rock-cut cave and the Hucchimalli temple are also prominent. The Archaeological Survey of India protects the site. Aihole is not itself a UNESCO World Heritage Site, although nearby Pattadakal is.

description: The Badami cave temples are a group of rock-cut sanctuaries in Badami, Bagalkot district, northern Karnataka, carved into a sandstone escarpment above the Agastya Teertha lake. They were excavated under the Early Chalukyas, who ruled from Badami, then called Vataapi, between the 6th and 8th centuries. Four main caves are numbered 1 to 4, each laid out as a verandah, pillared hall and inner sanctum, though the numbering does not strictly follow the order of excavation. Cave 1 is Shaiva and includes an eighteen-armed Nataraja relief. Caves 2 and 3 are chiefly Vaishnava, with a Trivikrama relief in Cave 2 and a Harihara figure in Cave 3. Cave 4, the smallest and added later, is Jain and holds Tirthankara images. Cave 3 is the best dated of the group, with an inscription corresponding to 578-579 CE that records its dedication by the ruler Mangalesha, and it retains some of the earliest surviving fresco traces in Karnataka. The caves blend northern Nagara and southern Dravida idioms and appear with Aihole and Pattadakal in a serial entry on UNESCO's Tentative List, 'Evolution of Temple Architecture'.

description: The Gommateshwara statue at Karkala in Udupi district, Karnataka, depicts Bahubali, revered in Jainism, in the standing kayotsarga meditation posture. It is carved from a single block of granite and rises about 42 feet on Gommata Betta hill. According to Wikipedia, an inscription records its consecration on 13 February 1432 CE, under Veera Pandya Bhairarasa Wodeyar of the Santara dynasty. The Udupi district tourism website gives the same year, says the project was guided by the Jain teacher Lalitakirti, and notes that a Brahma image on the brahmastambha (pillar) at the entrance was installed in 1436. The Udupi tourism website describes it as the second tallest monolithic statue in Karnataka. Wikipedia reports that the Archaeological Survey of India protects it as a monument of national importance, and that the Karkala Jain Math serves as its governing body. A ceremonial anointing, the Mahamastakabhisheka, is held roughly every twelve years, and the town is also home to several Jain basadis, including the Chaturmukha Basadi.

description: The Banashankari Amma Temple is at Cholachagudda in Badami taluk, Bagalkot district, Karnataka, a short distance from Badami. It is dedicated to Banashankari, a form of Parvati also called Shakambhari and Vanadurge. According to Wikipedia, she was the tutelary deity of the Chalukyas and is especially revered by the Devanga community. Historians cited there date the original temple to the 7th century CE, while the present rebuilt structure is attributed to a Maratha chieftain, Parusharam Agale, in 1750. The walled complex has a mukha mantapa, an ardha mantapa and a sanctum crowned by a vimana, in a style Wikipedia describes as Vijayanagara. The black stone image shows the goddess seated on a lioness with eight arms. A large square tank, Haridra Tirtha, lies at the entrance. The annual Banashankari jatre, held in January or February around the Rath Yatra, includes a chariot procession, the Teppotsava boat festival and a cattle fair.

description: Junagarh Fort is a palace-fort in Bikaner, Rajasthan, built under Raja Rai Singh, who ruled from 1571 to 1611. According to Wikipedia, its foundation ceremony took place in 1589 and the fort was completed in 1594, and later rulers added palaces and courtyards over about four centuries. Wikipedia notes that the complex contains temples of both Hindu and Jain traditions, the earliest dated to the 16th century. Among them is Har Mandir, described as the private chapel of the Bikaner royal family; sources differ on its principal deity. One visitor account also mentions a Ganesha shrine at Suraj Pol and a shrine to the goddess Kotashri, described as the protector of the fort. The shrines sit within a fort that is also a museum and heritage site.

description: Chandragiri, also called Chikkabetta, is the smaller of the two hills at Shravanabelagola in Hassan district, Karnataka, a major Jain pilgrimage centre. According to Wikipedia, about fourteen basadis (Jain temples) stand on it, among them the Chavundaraya, Chandragupta, Shantinatha and Parshvanatha basadis. Jain tradition associates the hill with the teacher Bhadrabahu and the Maurya emperor Chandragupta, who is said to have undertaken sallekhana (ritual fast) here; a Bhadrabahu cave and inscriptions are located on the hill, and Chandragupta's footprints are venerated there. The Chandragupta basadi, one of the smaller ones, is dedicated to Parshvanatha, with Padmavati and Kushmandini beside him. Wikipedia dates the main structure to roughly the 9th to 10th century, and its ornamental doorway and perforated screens to about the mid-12th century; the screen carvings are interpreted as scenes from the lives of Bhadrabahu and Chandragupta. According to Wikipedia, the Archaeological Survey of India has listed the Chandragupta basadi, within the Shravanabelagola group of monuments, as an Adarsh Smarak.

description: Chaturmukha Basadi is a Jain temple on Chikkabetta hill at Karkala in Udupi district, Karnataka, near the Gommateshwara (Bahubali) statue. The name means four-faced: the granite temple is symmetrical, with an identical doorway on each of its four sides and a square hall with pillared porticoes under a flat roof of large stone slabs. According to Wikipedia, an inscription dated 1586 CE records its construction by Immadi Bhairarasa Vodeya (Bhairava II) of the Kalasa-Karkala ruling family, calling it Tribhuvanatilaka Jina Chaityalaya, and records village endowments for daily worship and annual ceremonies. The sanctum holds life-size standing images of the Tirthankaras Aranatha, Mallinatha and Munisuvrata, along with other Tirthankara images. Karnataka Tourism describes 108 granite pillars. The Archaeological Survey of India protects the monument and carried out conservation work in 2006-07. Mahavir Jayanti and Das Lakshana are observed here.

description: The Chennakeshava Temple stands on the bank of the Yagachi river at Belur in Hassan district, Karnataka, about 35 km from Hassan town. It is dedicated to Vishnu as Chennakeshava, a name that inscriptions suggest replaced the earlier Vijayanarayana. The Hoysala king Vishnuvardhana commissioned it, and it was completed in 1117 CE, with further building continuing over roughly the next century. Wikipedia describes a soapstone shrine with a star-shaped plan on a raised circumambulatory platform, carved friezes of elephants, dancers, musicians and scenes from the epics and Puranas, and bracket figures known as madanikas, of which 38 of an original 40 survive. Queen Santala Devi is recorded as sponsor of the neighbouring Kappe Chennigaraya shrine. Under Harihara II of the Vijayanagara empire, a finial and a seven-storey brick gateway were added in the late 14th century. The temple remains in active Vaishnava worship, and in 2023 it was inscribed on the UNESCO World Heritage List as part of the Sacred Ensembles of the Hoysalas.

description: Dharmasthala, in Dakshina Kannada district of Karnataka, is a temple town in the Western Ghats whose main shrine honours Shiva as Manjunatha. According to Wikipedia, the complex blends Hindu and Jain elements, with shrines to the goddess Ammanavaru, the Tirthankara Chandraprabha and guardian deities; local tradition holds that these deities appeared to the chieftain Birmanna Pergade and his wife Ammu Ballalthi and asked to be worshipped here. According to Swarajya, worship is conducted by Vaishnava Brahmin priests, while a Jain family, the Heggades, has hereditary charge as dharmadhikari; Veerendra Heggade has held the role since 1968. Swarajya magazine describes the dharmadhikari's mandate in terms of four gifts: food, security, medicine and education, and reports that the associated trust runs over a hundred institutions across Karnataka. The same article notes the annual Lakshadeepotsava festival, which includes multi-faith and literary gatherings. The temple receives very large numbers of pilgrims each year.

description: Dodda Basavana Gudi, widely known as the Bull Temple, stands on Bull Temple Road in Basavanagudi, South Bengaluru, beside the Bugle Rock park. It is dedicated to Nandi (Basava), Shiva's bull mount and devotee. According to Wikipedia and Karnataka Tourism, it was built in 1537 by Kempe Gowda I, the founder of Bengaluru, in the Vijayanagara period; Wikipedia adds that the present tower over the shrine dates to the early twentieth century. The sanctum houses a monolithic granite Nandi about 4.6 m (15 ft) high and roughly 6 m (20 ft) long, its surface darkened by the regular application of charcoal and oil and coated with butter. A Dodda Ganesha shrine stands nearby. Every year in the month of Karthika the Kadalekai Parishe, or groundnut fair, fills the neighbourhood as devotees offer groundnuts. A popular legend, as retold by India TV, says a bull used to eat villagers' groundnut crops until the temple was built.

description: Ellora is a complex of rock-cut monuments carved into basalt cliffs near the village of Ellora, in the Aurangabad (Chhatrapati Sambhajinagar) area of Maharashtra. Thirty-four of the excavations are the ones usually visited. They are numbered from south to north: caves 1 to 12 are Buddhist, 13 to 29 are Hindu, and 30 to 34 are Jain. Most are dated between roughly the 6th and 11th centuries CE, though sources place the earliest Buddhist excavations considerably earlier and differ on the exact sequence. The site is valued for placing monasteries and shrines of three traditions side by side. Its best-known monument is the Kailasa temple (Cave 16), a Shiva temple that, according to Britannica, was excavated under the Rashtrakuta king Krishna I in the 8th century. Unlike most caves, it was cut downward from the top of a rock mass, leaving a freestanding structure with carved panels from the Ramayana and Mahabharata. Ellora was inscribed as a UNESCO World Heritage Site in 1983.

description: Cave 32, known as Indra Sabha, is one of five Digambara Jain caves at the northern end of the Ellora complex in Chhatrapati Sambhajinagar (formerly Aurangabad) district, Maharashtra, part of a UNESCO World Heritage Site inscribed in 1983. According to Wikipedia, it is a two-storey excavation with a monolithic shrine in its courtyard, dated to the 9th century. The name is regarded as a misnomer, since 19th-century writers mistook Jain yakshas for images of Indra. The upper level shows signs of continued Jain worship. Inside are an image of Ambika, the yakshi of Neminatha, seated on a lion beneath a mango tree, and a four-faced shrine in which Rishabhanatha, Neminatha, Parshvanatha and Mahavira face the cardinal directions. Jainpedia describes a standing Jina relief, probably Parshvanatha, shown unclothed in deep meditation in the Digambara manner, with a damaged serpent-hood canopy. Wikipedia also notes lotus carvings on the ceiling.

description: Ghati Subramanya is a Hindu temple near Tubagere in Doddaballapura taluk, about 60 km from Bengaluru in Karnataka. Its main image shows Lord Subramanya, also called Kartikeya or Murugan, shown beneath a seven-headed cobra and carved from a single stone, with Lord Narasimha carved on the reverse. The two deities face opposite directions, Subramanya east and Narasimha west, and a large mirror in the sanctum lets devotees see both together. Wikipedia and the Bengaluru Rural district website describe the temple as more than 600 years old, and the Incredible India page gives about 600 years; the sources say it was first developed by the Ghorpade rulers of Sandur, and both images are believed to be self-manifested. Local tradition links the name to the demon Ghatikasura. Many carved snake stones are installed around the temple, and devotees come for snake-related worship. Brahmarathotsava on Pushya Shuddha Shashti and Narasimha Jayanti are among its main festivals, and a cattle fair is held in December.

description: Mahabaleshwar Temple is a Shiva temple in the coastal town of Gokarna in Uttara Kannada district, Karnataka, close to the Arabian Sea beach. Its main lingam is known as the Atmalinga. According to tradition, Ravana received the Atmalinga from Shiva but Ganesha, disguised as a boy, set it on the ground at Gokarna, where it could not be moved and came to be called Mahabaleshwara. Wikipedia reports that the temple is traditionally linked to the Kadamba king Mayuravarma in the 4th century CE, and that the Sanskrit poet Kalidasa mentions the lord of Gokarna. Wikipedia describes a Dravidian-style granite complex, much of it from the Vijayanagara period (1336 to 1646). description: Kanaganahalli is an archaeological Buddhist site in Chittapur taluk of Kalaburagi district, Karnataka, on the left bank of the Bhima River and roughly 3 km from Sannati. The remains are generally dated between about the first century BCE and the third century CE, though some accounts place the earliest phase of the stupa in the Mauryan period, and the Archaeological Survey of India manages the site. Excavations uncovered a large brick stupa, referred to as a chaitya in inscriptions on the site, together with smaller memorial stupas and structures that may have belonged to a monastery. Carved limestone panels show Buddha footprints, Jataka scenes and Satavahana-era rulers, and the sculpture is described as bridging the Amaravati and Nagarjunakonda styles. Digs in the 1990s also yielded a relief inscribed Raya Asoko, widely read as a portrait of the Mauryan emperor Ashoka. Inscriptions and lead coins naming Satavahana rulers help date the stupa. The Archaeological Survey of India announced conservation work in 2022, and plans to develop Kanaganahalli and Sannati as a Buddhist heritage destination have been reported.

description: Kanakagiri, also called Kanakadri, is a Jain tirtha on a hill near Maleyur in Chamarajanagar district, Karnataka, about 53 km from Mysuru. description: Kappe Chennigaraya Temple is a Hoysala-era Vishnu shrine within the Chennakeshava Temple complex at Belur in Hassan district, Karnataka, on the south side of the main temple. description: The Kuda Caves are a group of rock-cut Buddhist monastic caves cut into a hill above Kuda village in Mangaon taluka of Raigad district, Maharashtra, near the Murud-Janjira coast. description: Kukke Subramanya Temple stands at Subramanya (formerly Kukke Pattana) in Kadaba taluk, Dakshina Kannada district, Karnataka, on the banks of the Kumaradhara river amid forest and Western Ghats hills. description: Lenyadri is a hill about five kilometres from Junnar in Pune district, Maharashtra, on which around thirty rock-cut caves were excavated. The shrine is counted among the eight Ashtavinayak temples of Maharashtra, and the caves are protected by the Archaeological Survey of India. Ganesh Chaturthi and Ganesh Jayanti are the main festivals.

description: The Mahalasa Narayani Temple stands at Mardol in Ponda taluka, Goa, and is dedicated to Mahalasa, identified with Mohini, the female form of Vishnu. Goud Saraswat Brahmins and Vaishnavas also call her Narayani, and in the Khandoba tradition she is regarded as a form of Parvati. According to Wikipedia, the original temple was at Velham (Verna) and was destroyed by the Portuguese in 1567, after which the icon was saved, moved to Mardol and reconsecrated in a temple built in the 17th century. Local legend, as recounted by the Incredible India site, tells of the goddess appearing at Verna and asking a man named Mhal Pai to build her a shrine. The complex has smaller shrines to Shantadurga and Lakshmi Narayan, wooden pillars, a tall brass lamp pillar and a large brass bell. The main annual celebrations are the Magha Jatra and Navaratri.

description: Shri Manguesh (Mangueshi) Temple stands at Priol in Ponda taluka, Goa, about 21 km from Panaji. It is dedicated to Shiva worshipped as Manguesh in the form of a linga, and is the family deity of many Goud Saraswat Brahmin families. According to local tradition, the deity was first installed at Kushasthali, present-day Cortalim. According to the Goa government's tourism page, the linga was moved from Kushasthali to Priol, then under Adil Shah's control, during the Portuguese Inquisition; temple records date the relocation to 1560. The Goa government page says the temple was rebuilt twice under the Marathas, again in 1890, and last in 1973, when a golden kalasha was fitted; Wikipedia adds that the Peshwas granted the village of Mangeshi to the temple in 1739. The complex has a seven-storey lamp tower, a large water tank and a hall for gatherings of several hundred people. Annual observances include Maha Shivaratri and a January-February jatra, when the deity is taken out in a palanquin.

description: Mangi-Tungi is a Digambar Jain pilgrimage site on two neighbouring hills, Mangi and Tungi, in Satana taluka of Nashik district, Maharashtra, roughly 125 km from Nashik city. Both peaks rise to about 1,300 metres. The site is described as a Siddha Kshetra, a place where, according to the Nirvanakand tradition, Rama, Hanuman, Sugriva and a vast number of other ascetics are held to have attained liberation. Cave shrines and temples are spread across the slopes, including caves associated with Chandraprabhu and Rama on Tungi and temples at the foot of the hills, one of them dedicated to Parshvanath. An inscription dated 1343 CE is reported in the Adinath cave. A 108-foot figure of Rishabhdev, called the Statue of Ahimsa, was consecrated in February 2016, and press reports say Guinness World Records recognised it as the world's tallest Jain statue. An annual fair is held in the month of Kartik.

description: The Manmodi Caves are a group of rock-cut excavations in basalt on a hill about 3 km south of Junnar in Pune district, Maharashtra. According to Wikipedia, they fall into three clusters, known as the Bhutalinga, Amba-Ambika and Bhimashankar groups, and include unfinished chaitya halls, cells and viharas. Wondermondo, a heritage catalogue, counts roughly 40 to 45 caves and dates the Buddhist excavations to about the 1st to 3rd centuries CE. A Brahmi inscription records a gift to the Buddhist Sangha by a Yavana donor named Chanda, and another, dated Saka year 46 (124 CE), names Ayama, a minister of the Western Satrap ruler Nahapana, as the donor of a mandapa and cistern. The facade of the main chaitya carries a fan of petal-shaped compartments with a Lakshmi-type figure and elephants bearing water jars. Later, one group was adapted for Jain worship and takes its name from a carving of the goddess Ambika. Many caves are unfinished, partly collapsed or silted.

description: The Shri Marikamba Temple in Sirsi, Uttara Kannada district, Karnataka, is dedicated to Marikamba, a regional form of the village goddess Mari who came to be identified with Durga as the slayer of the buffalo demon. The temple's own website gives the consecration as 1689 CE, while Wikipedia gives 1688. The sanctum holds an idol about seven feet tall showing the goddess; local tradition holds that it was recovered from a pond on the road to Hangal. According to the temple, the sanctum, gopura and main gateways were built between 1850 and 1875, and since 1955 a five-member board of trustees has administered it. The complex has wall paintings in the Kaavi style. Its biennial jatra, which the temple describes as lasting eight days, includes the Shiva and Marikamba wedding and the slaying of Mahishasura. According to kamat.com, a gradual local reform movement led by chief trustee S. N. Keshwain ended animal sacrifice at the temple, a change for which Mahatma Gandhi later commended Keshwain.

description: The Cheluvanarayana Swamy Temple stands at Melukote (Melkote) in Mandya district, Karnataka, below the rocky Yadavagiri hills that overlook the Kaveri valley. Its presiding deity is Cheluvanarayana, a form of Vishnu, and it is counted among the Vaishnava Abhimana Kshetras. According to Wikipedia, tradition credits the Vaishnava teacher Ramanuja with installing the image around 1099 CE, though inscriptions suggest worship here predates him. Bharat Temples dates his visit to December 1098 CE, and legend says he recovered the lost processional image. Later patrons include the Mysore rulers, linked to the Rajamudi and Krishnarajamudi crowns. Together with the older Vairamudi crown, whose donor is unknown, these are brought out during the annual Vairamudi festival, held around March or April, which features a chariot procession. Wikipedia notes the temple is administered by the Karnataka government's Hindu Religious and Charitable Endowments department.

description: Mudabidri (also spelt Moodabidri or Moodbidri) in Dakshina Kannada is a Jain pilgrimage town, sometimes called the Jain Kashi or Jain Varanasi of the South. It is said to have 18 Jain temples (basadis), most clustered near the Jain Matha, whose seat is held by the Charukeerthi Bhattaraka. The best known is the Tribhuvana Tilaka Chudamani Basadi, popularly the Saavira Kambada or thousand-pillar basadi. According to Wikipedia, it was begun in 1430 under the local chieftain Devaraya Wodeyar and took 31 years to build. It has seven mandapas, a stone lowest storey with two wooden upper storeys, a copper-clad sloping veranda roof and a 50 ft monolithic manastambha, and its sanctum holds an eight-foot panchadhatu image of Chandraprabha, the eighth tirthankara. Guru Basadi, also called Siddhanta Basadi, is traditionally dated to 714 CE, enshrines a black stone Parshvanatha, and is associated with the 12th-century palm-leaf Dhavala manuscripts.

description: The Murudeshwara Temple is a Shiva temple at Murdeshwar, a coastal town in Bhatkal taluk, Uttara Kannada district, Karnataka. It stands on Kanduka Hill, which juts into the Arabian Sea. According to the legend recorded on Wikipedia and Karnataka tourism material, Ravana received the Atmalinga from Shiva, and Ganesha, disguised as a boy, tricked him into setting it down. When Ravana tried to wrench it free, pieces were scattered; in the versions recorded, a piece of the linga or its covering fell at Murdeshwar, where the presiding linga is worshipped as Mridesa. A 20-storey Raja Gopura, completed in 2008 according to Wikipedia, has a lift to a viewing level. Beside the temple is a Shiva statue about 123 feet tall, which Wikipedia reports was funded by R. N. Shetty. Karnataka tourism material describes a cave museum beneath it presenting the legend, and says dress rules apply to visitors.

description: Sri Chamundeshwari Temple stands on Chamundi Hill, roughly 13 km from Mysuru city in Karnataka, at about 3,300 feet according to Wikipedia. It is dedicated to Chamundeshwari, a fierce form of the goddess Durga, regarded as the tutelary deity of the Mysuru Maharajas and revered in Karnataka as Nada Devi. Local tradition links the hill with the slaying of the demon Mahishasura, from whom the name Mysuru is said to derive. Wikipedia says the original shrine is thought to date from the Hoysala era in the 12th century and the tower from the 17th; the temple's own authority site says it grew in prominence after the Wodeyars rose to power in 1399 and describes a seven-tiered gopura crowned with seven golden kalashas, and says Krishnaraja Wodeyar III repaired the shrine in 1827 and built the present entrance gopura. A large granite Nandi, installed in 1664 according to Wikipedia, sits on the path up the hill. Fridays in the month of Ashadha and the Navaratri festival, linked to Mysuru Dasara, draw especially large gatherings.

description: The Srikanteshwara temple, also called Nanjundeshwara, is a Shiva temple in Nanjangud, Mysuru district, Karnataka, on the right bank of the Kapila (Kabini) river. The town is often called Dakshina Kashi, the Kashi of the South. The deity's name recalls the Puranic episode in which Shiva drank the halahala poison from the churning of the ocean. According to Wikipedia, the shrine began under the Ganga dynasty, with the sanctum attributed to the Chola period around the 11th century (the Karnataka Tourism site instead credits the Ganga dynasty) and the front mandapa to the Hoysala period in the 13th century. Vijayanagara rulers are credited with a brick-and-mortar tower and the Parvati and Narayana shrines, and the Wodeyars with the gopuram and several mandapas. The gopuram, about 120 feet high and described as having seven to nine tiers, was built in 1845 and is credited to Devajammanni, queen of Krishnaraja Wadiyar III; according to Wikipedia the complex measures roughly 385 by 160 feet. Tradition links Tipu Sultan to the temple: after his royal elephant is said to have recovered its sight, he offered a green stone lingam, associated with the name Hakim Nanjunda and displayed at the Girijakalyana festival. The Dodda Jaathre chariot festival draws large crowds.

description: The Omkareshwara Temple is a Shiva temple in Madikeri, the headquarters of Kodagu district in Karnataka. According to Karnataka Tourism and other accounts, it was built in 1820 by Lingarajendra II, the ruler of Kodagu, as an act of atonement for killing an innocent person; local tradition holds that on the advice of his priests he brought a Shivalinga from Kashi (Varanasi) and installed it, and the linga is worshipped as Omkareshwara. The building is unusual for a Hindu temple of the region. It combines elements of Kerala-style tiled roofing with a central dome and corner minarets, and has been described as showing Islamic and Gothic influences. Deccan Herald notes that it has no mukhamantapa or flagstaff, and that a granite nandi pedestal stands before the shrine. A large tank with a central mantapa lies within the premises and holds fish.

description: Pattadakal, also called Raktapura, lies on the west bank of the Malaprabha River in Bagalkot district, Karnataka. The complex is usually described as having ten major temples, nine Hindu, mostly Shaiva, and one Jain, built chiefly in the 7th and 8th centuries by the Early Chalukyas. Chalukya kings used the site for coronations, and the name is often translated as stone of coronation. The Virupaksha temple, built in the 740s CE in the Dravida style and sponsored by Queen Lokamahadevi, is the largest and most elaborate of the group. The Sangameshwara temple dates to the early 8th century and is described as left unfinished, while the Papanatha temple blends Dravida and Nagara forms. The Jain Narayana temple, probably of the 9th century, is dedicated to a single Jina. Pattadakal was inscribed as a UNESCO World Heritage Site in 1987, and UNESCO describes it as a harmonious blend of architectural forms from northern and southern India. description: Rishabhdeo, also known as Dhulev, is a town in Udaipur district, Rajasthan, about 65 km from Udaipur, and is home to the Kesariyaji Tirth, a Jain temple dedicated to the first Tirthankara, Rishabhanatha. description: Shree Shantadurga Temple stands at the foot of a hill in Kavale (Kavlem) village, Ponda taluka, Goa, about 30 km from Panaji. description: Shatrunjaya is a hill range near the town of Palitana in Bhavnagar district, Gujarat, and is regarded as one of the foremost pilgrimage places of Jainism, particularly in the Svetambara tradition. description: Shravanabelagola, in Channarayapatna taluk of Hassan district, Karnataka, is one of the major pilgrimage centres of Jainism, particularly in the Digambara tradition. description: Somnath Temple stands at Prabhas Patan, near Veraval, in Gir Somnath district on the Saurashtra coast of Gujarat. description: Sringeri is a hill town on the Tunga river in Chikkamagaluru district, Karnataka, and the seat of the Sharadamba temple, part of the Dakshinamnaya Sri Sharada Peetham. description: The Udupi Sri Krishna Matha is a Krishna temple and monastic centre on Car Street in Udupi, Karnataka. description: Saptashrungi Gad is a hill shrine near Vani village in Kalwan taluka, Nashik district, Maharashtra, roughly 60 km from Nashik city. It stands among seven peaks of the Sahyadri range, from which the goddess takes her name, Saptashrungi Nivasini, the dweller of the seven peaks. The image, about eight feet tall and carved into the rock face, shows an eighteen-armed form of Durga and is coated in vermilion. According to Wikipedia, the Devi Bhagavata Purana lists the hills as a Shakta pitha, and tradition counts the site as the half (ardha) Shakti Peeth among the 'three and a half' of Maharashtra, a classification that is debated. Pilgrims traditionally climb around 500 rock-cut steps, said to date from 1710. A funicular trolley, described in the press as the first of its kind in India, was introduced in 2018 and shortens the ascent to a few minutes. The Chaitrotsav fair, from Rama Navami to Chaitra Purnima, is described as its principal festival. The temple is administered by the Shree Saptashrung Niwasini Devi Trust, formed in 1975.

description: Varanga is a village in Karkala taluk, Udupi district, Karnataka, regarded as an important Jain centre and home to several basadis and a Jain matha. The best known is Kere Basadi, a lake temple reached by boat. Wikipedia dates it to the 12th century and says its principal deity is Parshvanatha, the 23rd Tirthankara; its chaturmukha image shows four Tirthankaras facing the cardinal directions, with a Padmavati idol in front. Neminatha Basadi, a stone temple with a thatched roof, enshrines a seated black image of Neminatha, the 22nd Tirthankara, and is stated by Wikipedia to date from the 9th century, while a local priest quoted by Deccan Herald puts it at about 1,200 years. Deccan Herald also reports a 1424 CE inscription recording a grant by Devaraya of Vijayanagara, a 45-foot manastambha, and a Chandranatha Basadi housing the Jain matha, said to be a branch of the Humcha matha. A five-day chariot festival is held in February.

description: Venur is a village on the Phalguni river in Belthangady taluk, Dakshina Kannada district, Karnataka, known for its monolithic statue of Bahubali, also called Gomateshwara, a figure revered in Jainism. The statue is usually given as about 38 feet tall, though some reports say 35 feet. The statue faces west from a raised platform beside the river. It is traditionally attributed to the Jain ruler Thimmanna Ajila, said to be a descendant of Chamundaraya, who is credited with the Shravanabelagola statue, and it is dated to 1604. The sculptor is named as Jakanachari. According to local lore, the Ajilas hid the image under the river sand to stop it being taken to Karkala before they installed it. Venur is described as the capital of the Ajila dynasty, reported to have ruled from 1154 to 1786. Wikipedia counts it among five Bahubali monoliths in Karnataka taller than 20 feet. A Mahamastakabhisheka, the ceremonial anointing of the statue, is held periodically, with editions listed in 1928, 1956, 2000, 2012 and 2024.

description: The Vighneshwar temple at Ozar, on the Kukadi River in Junnar taluka of Pune district, is one of the eight Ashtavinayak shrines of Maharashtra dedicated to Ganesha, who is worshipped here as Vighneshwar or Vighnahar, the remover of obstacles. According to the Puranic legend recorded on Wikipedia, Ganesha subdued the obstacle-demon Vignasura, and sages then consecrated his image at this spot. The east-facing complex stands within a walled courtyard entered through a large gateway guarded by stone dvarapala figures, with stone lamp towers and a corridor of cusped arches. The sanctum image is described as self-manifested, with a left-turning trunk, flanked by brass figures of Siddhi and Riddhi. The shikhara is covered in gold; Wikipedia credits this to Chimaji Appa, the Peshwa Baji Rao I's brother, after his capture of Vasai Fort from the Portuguese, and notes a renovation in 1967. Ganesh Chaturthi, Ganesh Jayanti and a Kartik Poornima festival are observed.

description: The Vigneshwara (also called Vighnahar) Ganapati temple stands at Ozar on the Kukadi River, about 85 km from Pune near Narayangaon, in the Junnar area of Pune district, Maharashtra. It is one of the eight Ganesha shrines of the Ashtavinayak circuit. According to Wikipedia, the pilgrimage places Ozar seventh in the prescribed order, though many pilgrims visit it fifth for convenience of route. According to the legend cited by Wikipedia, Ganesha defeated Vignasura, the demon of obstacles, who then asked that Ganesha be called Vigneshwara, Lord of Obstacles, and the sages consecrated the image here. The east-facing temple has a walled courtyard, a gateway with two guardian figures, two lamp towers (deepamala) and a gilded shikhara. Its central image is regarded as self-manifested and is flanked by brass figures of Siddhi and Riddhi. Wikipedia states the shrine was renovated by Chimaji Appa, brother of Peshwa Baji Rao I, and again in 1967. Ganesh Chaturthi and Ganesh Jayanti are major festivals, and a five-day festival begins on Kartik Poornima.

description: The Vittala (Vitthala) Temple is one of the major monuments of Hampi, the former Vijayanagara capital, now part of the UNESCO World Heritage Group of Monuments at Hampi in Karnataka. It is dedicated to Vitthala, a form of Vishnu. The Incredible India portal dates it to the 15th century under the Vijayanagara Empire, while accounts differ on whether Deva Raya II or Krishnadevaraya was its principal patron, with later rulers adding to it. Its best-known feature is the stone chariot, a shrine to Garuda, Vishnu's mount, set on large wheels with two elephants in front; Karnataka Tourism dates it to the 16th century and says it was damaged by an invading army late in the empire's history. The main hall is also known for its pillars, which tradition says give out musical notes when struck, and which Incredible India describes as the SaReGaMa pillars. The chariot appears on the Indian 50-rupee note.
